subject: Vocabulary
topic: Phrasal Verbs — Meaning and Usage in Context (W11 B1)

questions.stem:
Choose the meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence:
'The negotiations BROKE DOWN after several hours of discussion.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. BREAK DOWN = to fail, collapse, or cease to function. 'The negotiations broke down' = they failed to reach an agreement. Other uses: 'The car broke down on the highway' (stopped working); 'She broke down and cried' (lost emotional control). Trap: 'postponed' confuses breakdown with adjournment; 'became more intense' is the opposite.

questions.stem:
Choose the meaning of the phrasal verb in the sentence:
'She GAVE UP trying to convince him after repeated failures.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. GIVE UP = to stop trying; to surrender or quit. 'She gave up trying' = she stopped making efforts. Other uses: 'He gave up smoking' (abandoned a habit); 'The soldiers gave up' (surrendered). Trap: all distractors imply continued or increased effort — opposite of 'give up'.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct meaning of 'CALL OFF' in context:
'The match was CALLED OFF due to heavy rain.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. CALL OFF = to cancel something that was planned. 'The match was called off' = the match was cancelled. Compare with CALL FOR (= require/demand), CALL ON (= visit or request), CALL OUT (= shout or expose). Trap: 'delayed by an hour' = postponed, not cancelled; 'moved to a different venue' = rescheduled, not cancelled.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct meaning of 'LOOK INTO' in the sentence:
'The committee will LOOK INTO the allegations of misconduct.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. LOOK INTO = to investigate or examine something carefully. 'Look into the allegations' = investigate the allegations. Compare: LOOK FOR (= search for), LOOK AFTER (= take care of), LOOK UP TO (= admire/respect), LOOK DOWN ON (= consider inferior). Trap: 'ignore' and 'dismiss' are the opposites of investigation.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct phrasal verb to complete the sentence:
'The factory has ___ of raw materials and will have to shut down temporarily.'
questions.explanation: A is correct. RUN OUT OF = to have no more of something; to exhaust a supply. 'Run out of raw materials' = no raw materials left. Compare: RUN OVER (= hit with a vehicle; or to overflow), RUN INTO (= encounter unexpectedly or collide), RUN AWAY (= flee/escape). Trap: 'run over' can mean 'overflow' but the context is about exhaustion of supply, not overflow.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct meaning of 'PUT OFF' in the sentence:
'The meeting has been PUT OFF until next Monday.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. PUT OFF = to postpone; to delay to a later time. 'Put off until next Monday' = delayed to Monday. Note the contrast with CALL OFF (cancelled permanently). PUT OFF can also mean 'to discourage or repel someone' (e.g., 'His rudeness put me off'). Trap: 'cancelled permanently' = call off, not put off; the phrase 'until next Monday' signals rescheduling, not cancellation.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct meaning of 'SET ASIDE' in the sentence:
'The judge SET ASIDE the earlier verdict.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. SET ASIDE (in legal contexts) = to nullify, overturn, or quash an order or verdict. 'The judge set aside the earlier verdict' = the judge nullified it. SET ASIDE also means 'to reserve or put away' in everyday use (e.g., 'set aside ₹500 for emergencies'). Trap: 'deferred' = postponed (not nullified); 'confirmed' = upheld (opposite of set aside in law); 'read aloud' = is irrelevant.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct meaning of 'COME ACROSS' in the sentence:
'I CAME ACROSS an interesting article while browsing the library.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. COME ACROSS = to find or encounter someone/something unexpectedly. 'Came across an article' = found it by chance. COME ACROSS can also mean 'to give an impression' (e.g., 'She comes across as confident'). Compare: COME OVER (= visit/move), COME AROUND (= change one's opinion), COME UP (= arise/occur). Trap: 'argued about' confuses 'across' with a confrontation meaning; 'wrote carefully' is entirely unrelated.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct phrasal verb to complete the sentence:
'The young leader quickly ___ as someone who commands respect and admiration.'
questions.explanation: C is correct. CAME ACROSS = gave the impression of being. 'Came across as someone who commands respect' = was perceived as such. This is the second meaning of 'come across' — to appear or seem a certain way to others. CAME OVER = visited (person moved to a place); CAME UP = arose/was raised (an issue came up); CAME AROUND = changed opinion or regained consciousness. Trap: 'came over' could colloquially mean 'appeared as', but 'came across as' is the standard SSC/formal usage for this sense.

questions.stem:
Choose the correct meaning of 'BEAR OUT' in the sentence:
'The evidence BORE OUT the defendant's claim of innocence.'
questions.explanation: B is correct. BEAR OUT = to support, confirm, or corroborate. 'The evidence bore out the claim' = the evidence confirmed/supported the claim. Other 'bear' phrasal verbs: BEAR WITH (= be patient with), BEAR OUT (= confirm), BEAR DOWN ON (= press hard/advance on), BEAR UP (= cope/remain strong). Trap: 'contradicted' is the exact opposite of what 'bore out' means; 'brought to public attention' confuses 'bear out' with 'bring out'.
